Good afternoon. The 104th Plenary Meeting of the General Assembly is called to order. I declare open the high-level meeting of the Assembly on Improving Global Road Safety under the overall theme of scaling up and accelerating implementation of commitments to halving road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030. This meeting is held in accordance with Resolution 80/247 of March 10th, 2026, And takes place under Agenda Item 12 entitled Improving Global Road Safety. The documentation under this item is listed in the Journal of the United Nations. I will now make a statement as the President of the General Assembly. Welcome to this high-level meeting of the General Assembly on Global Road Safety. Obviously, since you're here, it means that each of you had to navigate the streets of Manhattan to reach First Avenue. Whether you came by car, by bike, or simply walked, you were nonetheless part of the complex choreography of New York's traffic system. And while I'm sure, or at least I hope, you were paying attention to your surroundings, it is reassuring for each of us that the system required to keep that environment operating smoothly and safely are in place. We trust that there are rules and standards, laws and policy that make navigation roads possible, whether here in New York, in New Delhi, or in Nigeria. Most of the time we barely think about those systems. We simply assume that They will work. Traffic lights turning from red to green, sometimes in between yellow in some parts of the world. But while most journeys end safely, far too many do not. When I was a child, I personally remember my mother telling me about her sister. My aunt had died. It had been raining and she ran to the store to buy a ruler. She was hit by a tram when she was still a child. She died before I was born, so I never mourned her personally. But the legacy of that loss lingered. It shaped my grandparents, it shaped my mother, and it became one of those stories parents tell all their children, hoping they might take just a little more care when they just go out to buy a ruler. I forgot about this story, but I thought about that just last month here next to the General Assembly during our multi-stakeholder hearing on road safety, because one of the participants Ms. Vivian Perón, spoke about exactly this mourning and this situation for her own family, about losing her child, her son Kevin, 24 years ago in Argentina, but still feeling it till that day. She described what she called the never-ending ripples of devastation and how she continues to carry his agonizing absence in her heart. Listening to her, I think all of us who were in the room, we were reminded that while every road fatality is recorded as a statistic, every single one leaves behind a family like us whose lives are never quite the same again. And I know some of you may nevertheless be asking, well, why is this the United Nations' focus on road safety? Aren't there wars that need to be addressed? Is this really a priority of the United Nations? And frankly speaking, this question is understandable, and this is why we have to speak about it, because peace and security is for sure one of our most essential pillars. But it is not the only one. If we look back to the Charter as we did a couple of weeks ago, our responsibility is also to protect lives on a daily basis, to protect health and to promote well-being. And the stark reality, as highlighted by the Special Envoy, is that road traffic crashes have become A silent pandemic. Every year, more than 1.2 million people are killed on our roads just doing daily life, and another 50 million are injured. Think about these numbers. That is more than the number killed in direct conflict. That is more than the number of people murdered, more than the number who die from malaria. That means every 24 seconds another person loses their life on or because of the roads and highways. So since I began speaking, at least half a dozen more families like Vivian's have received news that will change their lives forever. The tragedy is not simply the scale of these losses. The tragedy is also the fact that different than other deadly global challenges, so many of them are entirely preventable. Therefore, it is so important to raise road safety also right here in this hall. Especially where, for once, we are dealing with an issue far from contentious. As for all the issues we discuss in this hall and for all the divisions that can sometimes arise, I guess nobody is against the desire to keep our families, the ones we love, safe while going to work or to school. As I also suspect, there are very few people in this hall who have not been touched by a similar story, by this silent pandemic, as Ms. Vivian Perrone. Whether it was a family member, a friend, or a neighbor, most of us know someone whose life changed forever because the journey that should have ended safely did not. And none of, none of us wants our children playing beside dangerous roads. None of us wants to drive cars that fail basic safety standards. None of us wants to see pedestrians, cyclists, or motorists suffer because of their poor infrastructure or preventable negligence. And none of us, speaking as a woman, understands why airbags, who are supposed to protect our bodies, are designed for men, so they're actually hurting women. many of the female drivers in a car crash. So this progress declaration before us, shepherded by our esteemed co-facilitators, Ambassador Aida Kazymalievaya of Kyrgyzstan and Ambassador Peter Olenyi of Slovakia, offers practical recommendations that can make a real difference. It calls for stronger national leadership on road safety in their own sovereignty, but in the understanding of being better together. Better by collecting data and use data together. Better in securing safer roads and vehicles. Improved post-crash response. And greater investment in road safety education. There's nothing contentious about any of this. So, dear colleagues, distinguished representatives, let us capitalize on this moment of unity and this rare opportunity for consensus. Let us commit to this declaration and, more importantly, to delivering on its 48 recommendations, not only in this hall but out there, on 42nd Street, in New Delhi, or in Nigeria, in every city, big or small, in every community. Let us do it for ourselves and for those we love, for our children on their way to school, and for parents like Vivian Perrone who continue to carry the absence of a child every single day. I thank you. Thank you.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, I'd like to thank the President of the General Assembly, Excellency Mrs. Annalena Baerbock, for convening this high-level meeting on road safety. I'm pleased to address you today on behalf of the United Nations Secretary-General. 10 years ago, I warned this Assembly that road crashes were one of the great emergencies of our time, a silent pandemic. In 2016, one person lost their life on the road every 25 seconds. More than 90% of those deaths occurred in low- and middle-income countries. We adopted an ambitious objective to reduce road traffic deaths and injuries by 50%. Today, hardly anything has changed. Between 2010 and 2021, road deaths declined by only 5%. The verdict is clear: we are far off track. Resolutions have been adopted, Commitments have been made, declarations have been endorsed, but actions are still too poor. Between today and the end of this year, more than 84,000 children will be killed on the road. The global economy will lose another $1.6 trillion. None of this is inevitable. In my UN capacity, I've traveled to more than 100 countries. I visited hospitals filled with people whose lives have been changed forever by road crashes. I've spoken with grieving family members after they lost a child. They may not understand why their loved one was taken from them. We do. They are the consequences of not acting enough. 8 years ago, the American President Harry Truman reminded leaders that confronting road crashes required leadership and responsibility at every level of society. Unfortunately, we are still learning the same lessons today. We understand the risk— speeding, driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, distracted driving, and the failure to use proper helmets. Seatbelts, and child restraints. The solutions are equally clear: safer infrastructure, safer vehicles, lower speeds, stronger enforcement, better post-crash care. The challenge has never been knowing what to do. It has been finding the determination to do it. This year, we have passed the second midpoint of the second decade of action for road safety. We cannot afford to continue at our current pace. On the world's road, business as usual is a business of death. In the next 5 years, the number of motor vehicles worldwide is expected to increase nearly 25%, placing enormous pressure on transport systems already struggling with rapid urban growth. Without decisive action, we will face more congestion, worse pollution, greater inequality, and more preventable deaths. By 2050, nearly 17% of the world's population will live in cities. This demands a different vision for mobility, where roads are designed for people instead of vehicles, public transport is prioritized, and every child can travel safely to school, and every worker can return home safe. Governments have the primary responsibility. Today, road safety observatories do exist but are under-equipped. Every country should establish a lead road safety agency with the authority, resources, and political support to coordinate action across government. Governments must also know where lives are being lost. Strong national crash data systems are essential to identify risk, measure progress, and direct investment where they will have the greatest impact. Safe speed limits must be adopted and enforced, particularly around school and residential areas. National legislation should be aligned with United Nations road safety conventions and internationally agreed vehicle safety standards. Urban planners and engineers must ensure that safety is built into every road design. And as micromobility devices transform our cities, our policies and enforcement must evolve with them. We also need the private sector in the fight, not only by complying with the law, but by driving safety innovation. Companies should embed safety throughout their fleets, products, supply chains, and business practices. For example, every motorcycle should be sold with 2 UN-certified helmets. If cars come with seatbelts, motorcycles should come with helmets. We know that safe helmets can be produced for below $20. Far more of these helmets must be manufactured in markets where they are most needed. Every passenger car, wherever it is sold and operates, must meet universally agreed safety and inspection standards. No aircraft manufacturer will consider fitting aircraft with different safety features based on the market they serve. The same must apply to vehicles worldwide. We also need academia and civil society to continue generating evidence and demanding accountability. International organizations must advance global cooperation and help countries transform knowledge into action. And young people need to be at the center of our work because they pay the highest price. Road crashes continue to be the number one killer of people aged 5 to 29. That is completely unacceptable. We have the prescription and the vaccine, but too often we are still not using them. There are encouraging examples Some countries have significantly reduced fatality rates in just a few years. But for each of them, this was only achieved through making road safety a serious national priority. Those decisions have saved many lives. Across the UN system, progress is accelerating. Agencies throughout the UN family are recognizing the urgency of road crashes. The World Health Organization is improving fatality reporting and ensuring that road safety is internationally recognized as a public health and development priority. UNECE is providing clear guidance and regulation for AI and automation in transport as a global custodian for vehicle safety. The United Nations Road Safety Fund is helping governments turn commitments into results. Earlier today, the Road Safety Funds Partnership Pledging Conference brought together member states, UN agencies, and the private sector to increase support for the only UN pooled funding mechanism dedicated to road safety. These are encouraging actions, but they need to be matched by stronger political leadership and serious investment. Developed countries must extend greater support to those carrying the heaviest burden. And we must build more creative partnerships across sectors. In my office, the Special Envoy Group of Friends is a network of over 120 leaders from government, industry, international organizations, and celebrities committed to supporting global road safety. With the advertising company JCDecaux, we have developed the global campaign for road safety, which is present in nearly 80 countries and southern cities worldwide. The ambition of our partnerships must match the scale of the problem. Over the next 2 days, I look forward to hearing say your new commitments, but commitments alone are not enough. The crisis will end when our actions demonstrate that the loss of young life is not an acceptable cost of living in a modern world. 78 years ago, this Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Article 3 stipulates that everyone has a right to life, liberty, and security of person. Safe mobility is not only an issue of transport or healthy policy. It is a question of whether we choose to uphold our most fundamental rights. Together, we can finally address the silent pandemic on our roads for all people because every delay costs too many lives. Thank you, Madam President.
I thank the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Road Safety. I now give the floor to His Excellency Lok Bahadur Thapa, President of the Economic and Social Council.

President of the General Assembly, Secretary-General, Special Envoy for Road Safety, Director-General of WHO, Excellencies, Distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, it is a pleasure to join you today for this high-level meeting on road safety. Excellencies, road safety is often discussed as a transport issue. It is of course that, but it is much more than that. Clearly, it is a development issue, it is a public health issue, on social justice issues, and climate issues. Ultimately, it is about implementing the Sustainable Development Goals in ways that improve people's lives. This meeting comes just days after the conclusion of the High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development, where Member States examined how to accelerate The implementation of Sustainable Development Goal 11. The review of SDG 11 reaffirmed that transport cannot be considered in isolation. It must be planned alongside housing, land use, and public space if cities are to become more inclusive, more resilient, Road safety illustrates this well. It is shaped not only by how we design our cities and mobility systems, but by the choices we make about how people move safely through them. Road safety also illustrates the value of the ECOSOC mandate. Our role is to bring together the economic, social, and environmental dimensions of sustainable development. Transport decisions have consequences far beyond the transport sector. They shape public health, they shape urban development, economic opportunities, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. They therefore require coordinated actions across sectors. As we have heard, every year more than 1.2 million people lose their lives on the roads, with the overwhelming majority occurring in low- and middle-income countries. Millions suffer— more suffer life-changing injuries. We all know that behind every statistic is a human story, a person's, a family's, a community's, whose future is forever altered. 8. These tragedies are not inevitable. They are preventable. Transport may not have its own Sustainable Development Goal, but it is an indispensable enabler of sustainable development. It connects people to education, It connects to jobs and opportunities, and it connects to healthcare. It supports economic growth, and it supports social inclusion and resilient communities. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the recently proclaimed United Nations Decade for Sustainable Transport for 2026-2035 reinforces Rather than advancing the parallel tracks, the Decade of Sustainable Transport and the Decade of Action for Road Safety should inform a single approach to transport, one that places safety at the heart of sustainable mobility. What does this mean in practice? It means planning housing, transport, and public sector space together rather than in isolation. It means building safety into transport planning from the outset, rather than trying to correct dangerous systems after tragedy strikes. This is also the essence of the Safe System Approach— designing transport systems that recognize human vulnerability and ensure that mistakes do not result in death or serious injury. We also need to rethink how we measure success. For decades, success has been defined by how efficiently we move vehicles. The true measures of success should instead be whether people, especially children, older persons, persons with disabilities, pedestrians, and cyclists, can move safely, affordably, and with dignity. Let us seize this opportunity to build transport systems that put people first. Let us act with urgency, with ambition, and with solidarity, because every life saved on our roads brings us one step closer to the promise of the 2030 Agenda. a future that is safer, more inclusive, and more sustainable for all. The Economic and Social Council remains committed to supporting international cooperation and partnership that advance road safety. I thank Kyrgyzstan and Slovakia for their leadership in negotiating it. It means designing streets for people first, not motor vehicles. It means accepting that people make mistakes and taking action to ensure those mistakes aren't deadly. It means doing more to protect people who walk, cycle, or ride a motorbike because their lives matter as much as anyone traveling behind the wheel. This is not a job for the health sector alone. We need academia, civil society, and the media to produce evidence and hold leaders to account. We need youth movements to demand action and help us take it, because too often it's their generation paying the highest price. If we do this, the rewards are immense. Every step and every ride reduces the risk of heart disease, diabetes and cancer. And if we give them the chance, more people choose public transport. This is an encouraging sign of the international community's willingness to redouble its efforts and make progress towards meeting the global road safety goals and prevent avoidable loss of life. Traffic accidents are a major public health issue with more than 1 million people losing their lives as a result of it every year globally, and this is why in Uruguay we put people and the protection of life at the heart of our public policies. We hold the certainty that road safety must be integrated into health policy, transport policy, education, urban development, and infrastructure policy with a vision that is underpinned by evidence, with institutional leadership, and a sustained commitment from state and society. In this regard, UNICEF has strengthened its role as the governing body of national road safety policy in Uruguay, fostering coordination across national agencies, subnational governments, enforcement agencies, the justice system, academia, and civil society. For us, governance constitutes the main instrument for achieving results. Within this framework, we have developed a work plan with 6 strategic lines that we have been actively applying and developing. Firstly, strengthening the presence road safety on the public agenda by promoting a culture of prevention and respect. Secondly, by deepening oversight and effective compliance with the rules. This includes coordination between the distinct levels of governments and different institutions. Thirdly, expanding social and territorial participation. This allows us to identify concrete specific problems and to design solutions adapted to the realities in the country. And these 3 initiatives together have allowed us to reduce deaths by 12.5% in the first half of this year. Fourthly, incorporating road safety into the education program. Fifth, strengthening a response of the justice system, seeking a coherent and effective implementation of the regulations. And finally, continue developing specific management tools such as the points-based driver's license, speed management, and other systems. Uruguay also gives special importance to international and regional cooperation. Currently, we hold the presidency of the Ibero-American Road Safety Observatory. This is a network made up of 22 Ibero-American countries. This promotes exchange of experiences, strengthening technical capacity, and the production of comparable information, as well as the development of common public policy for the region. In June 2026, we'll approve the Madrid Declaration. This will be submitted to heads of state and government. We know that achieving the Global Goals requires political leadership. I thank you.
The distinguished representative of Uruguay. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Greece.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, Greece fully supports the objective of the Second Decade of Action for Road Safety to reduce road traffic deaths and injuries by at least 50% by 2030. For us, this is not only an international target, it is a national commitment. and it is measured in lives. Road safety is not only a transport issue. It is public health, law enforcement, infrastructure, education, and above all, culture. In Greece, we have chosen to move from commitments to implementation. We adopted a new road traffic code focused on the behaviours that cost lives— speeding, alcohol, non-use of helmets and seatbelts, red light violations, and dangerous driving. We have strengthened enforcement through targeted police controls and the deployment of AI road cameras. At the same time, we are making safe choices easier. In Athens, 24-hour public transport every Saturday night helps thousands of people, especially young people, return home safely after going out. We are also investing in safer infrastructure, with major upgrades across the national road network and new projects currently under construction. These efforts are producing results. In 2025, Greece recorded 517 road fatalities, the lowest number since 1963, and one of the strongest reductions in fatal crashes in Europe. But we are not satisfied. Every life lost is one too many. Our next priorities are clear: protecting motorcyclists and pedestrians, tackling speeding and drink-driving, improving safety during peak travel periods, and using better data to guide every intervention. Greece is advancing an integrated national road safety strategy that brings together government, local authorities, police, infrastructure operators, and civil society. We believe that effective governance, reliable data, and accountability are essential to saving lives. Our message today is simple: road deaths Accidents are not inevitable, they are preventable. The 2030 target will not be achieved through declarations alone. It will be achieved through implementation, enforcement, safer infrastructure, better data, and international cooperation. Greece remains fully committed to contributing to this common effort, sharing our experience and learning from others.

Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Greece. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic.

Your Excellency, Madam President of the General Assembly of the United Nations, on behalf of the Dominican Republic, I want to say that I'm grateful for this opportunity to participate in this high-level meeting on road safety. This is an issue that calls on our responsibility as governments as well as an international community. We express our support and our readiness and support for the declaration adopted today. It calls on us to take on this global commitment. Allow me to begin with a reality that can leave no one indifferent. In the year 2025, 2,992 individuals lost their lives in traffic accidents in the Dominican Republic. More than 65% of them, precisely 1,995 of them, were motorcyclists. And this is why we are implementing a new technical norm of approved standardized helmets, which guarantees that only helmets able to— capable of saving lives for the driver and the passenger enter the country. At the same time, we are working to ensure that in the Dominican Republic, no motorcycle is sold without a certified helmet. And we have a slogan for this: one motorcycle, one helmet.

On—

in November 2024, our president signed the National Pact for Road Safety, signed by 121 public and private entities. And road safety has been declared a priority of high national interest through Decree 656/24. This also initiated the National Strategic Road Safety Plan 2025 through 2030. Road safety also requires the involvement of young people, and this is why, in coordination with the of Education, we have launched the Traffic Guardians Program where all high school students this year will take virtual education— virtual practice for road safety with the aim of achieving 300,000 students trained by 2028. Road safety is not, however, the exclusive responsibility of governments. It requires a commitment from civil society and also from academia. This is why we are working to ensure that private companies also implement road safety labor plans. The Dominican Republic, we are reaffirming our commitment to this global agenda. We will continue acting decisively and to continue to place the protection of life at the center of every public policy. There is no great— more noble mission than saving lives. I thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kenya.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, road safety remains one of Kenya's foremost public health and development challenges. Over the last 5 years, Kenya has continued to record approximately 4,000 to 5,000 road fatalities annually, with more than 20,000 people injured. We recognize the burden of road safety— road traffic injuries remains unacceptably high. Vulnerable road users, particularly pedestrians and motorcyclists, account for majority of these fatalities, together contributing well over half the deaths on our roads. Road crashes are not only transport issue, but economic and social development issue. Kenya estimates that road traffic crashes account for 5% of the GDP annually. In response to this challenge, Kenya has embraced a safe system approach anchored on 3 pillars, basically, of implementation: engineering, enforcement, and education. We continue to invest in safer road infrastructure through emphasis on non-motorized transport facilities, road safety audits, safer school zones, and the adaptation of international road safety assessment standards. In enforcement, we strengthened evidence-based enforcement through technology-based traffic management, improved driver vehicle regulations, and enhanced compliance monitoring. We also modernized driver licensing and vehicle inspection and digital enforcement system to improve accountability. Education In education, public awareness remains central to our strategy. Kenya has intensified nationwide road safety campaigns targeting schools, public transport operators and employers, communities, and vulnerable road users. We are embedding road safety education into learning institutions while promoting behavioral change among road users. Implementation of National Road Safety Action Plan aligned UN Decade of Action for Road Safety is also a key pillar of our approach. We therefore welcome today's adoption of progress declaration of the high-level meeting on improving road— global road safety as an important international milestone and look forward to implementing it. Your Excellencies, Kenya remains fully committed to delivering safer roads through stronger partnership, smarter technologies, safer infrastructure, effective enforcement, and sustained public education. And at the core of this approach is partnership, where we look forward to continued collaboration with all of you and ensure a safer road for all. Together, through shared commitment and global cooperation, we can save lives, protect livelihoods, build safer, more sustainable transport systems for the present and future generations. Thank you.

Thank you.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, Japan welcomes the adoption of the progress declaration which emphasizes stronger governance and evidence-based action with accountability through follow-up and monitoring. Road safety is a matter of the utmost importance to Japan as a dimension of human well-being and sustainable development. Over the past decades, Japan has achieved a substantial reduction in road traffic fatalities by comprehensively addressing road safety, focusing on human vehicles and mobility systems and the road environment. This progress has been achieved through a sustained whole-of-government approach grounded in clear legal mandates, institutionalized coordination across ministries and the level of government Supported by the active engagement of the private sector and civil society. As a result, Japan now records the lowest level of road traffic fatalities in its history. Japan's approach rests on 3 mutually reinforcing pillars. The first is a robust governance framework. Japan's road safety system is anchored in the Basic Act on Traffic Safety Measures, which defines responsibilities across all levels of government and provides a legal basis for successive 5-year national plans and provides— which defines the responsibilities of government and provides legal basis for successive 5-year national plans. The National Council for Traffic Safety Measures, chaired by the Prime Minister, ensures high-level political leadership and cross-ministerial coordination. Fostering shared responsibility to translate national policy into concrete measures at both national and subnational levels. Japan's 12th Traffic Safety Basic Plan, launched in April this year, is grounded in this framework and sets forth targets and measures through 2030, adapted to new societal challenges including emerging demographic and technical changes. The second is evidence-based policymaking. Structured data collection and analysis enables the identification of risk, targeted interventions, and measurement of outcomes. The third is a human-centered approach to traffic safety, supported by lifelong traffic safety education and public awareness raising. As society and the mobility environment become increasingly diverse and complex, Japan is placing greater emphasis on tailored measures that reflect the different needs, behaviors, and the risk of road users, including older persons, children, pedestrians, cyclists, users of new forms of mobility, and foreign visitors and residents. Reflecting this approach, in partnership with subnational governments, civil societies, the Government of Japan has promoted nationwide road safety campaigns. In closing, Japan remains fully committed to advancing global road safety through the utmost collective efforts of the government and private sector.

Thank you.

Thank you.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the government and the people of the Republic of Sierra Leone, I extend our profound gratitude to the President of the General Assembly for convening this important high-level meeting under the theme Scaling Up and Accelerating Implementation of Commitment to Halving Road Traffic deaths and injuries by 2030. It requires us to assess whether our actions at the national, regional, continental, and global level have been translated to safer roads for all users. Sierra Leone aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the African group, the African Union has demonstrated leadership by positioning member states to domesticate and implement the Africa Road Safety Charter in line with its Agenda 2063. In West Africa in particular, the ECOWAS Road Safety Charter is enforced, which is in line with the group's Vision 2050. Under the visionary leadership of His Excellency the President, Dr. Julius Maada Bio, President of the Republic of Sierra Leone, outgoing Chairman of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government, and coordinator of the Africa Union Committee of 10 on UN Security Council reform, road safety has been integrated into our Medium-Term National Development Plan 2024-2030. We call for strengthening regional and continental mechanisms to support member states, particularly in low- and medium-income countries. to reduce the vulnerability to road traffic injuries. Madam President, Sierra Leone remains committed to the Second Decade of Action for Road Safety, 2021 to 2030.

Thank you.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, distinguished delegates, on behalf of the Republic of Serbia, I would like to reaffirm our strong commitment to improving global road safety and achieving the targets of the second decade of action. Serbia fully supports the global road safety framework established through the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Global Plan for the Decade of Action for Road Safety, and the relevant United Nations resolutions. Our national road safety policy is based on the safe system approach and on the principle that no death or serious injury on our roads is acceptable. In line with this vision, Serbia's National Road Safety Strategy 2023-2030 sets ambitious goals to reduce road traffic fatalities and serious injuries by 50% by 2030 and to achieve Vision Zero for children, with the ultimate objective that no child loses their life in road traffic. In the past decade, Serbia has been building highways with highest safety standards, but what we realize is that protecting children and vulnerable road users requires more than legislation and infrastructure. We help children develop safe behavior from an early age and create a strong road safety culture for future generations.

Thank you.

Effective governance and multisectoral coordination are at the core of our efforts. National Road Safety Coordination Body established by the government brings together 7 ministries and the Road Traffic Safety Agency, ensuring action across all relevant sectors. This cooperation is further strengthened through partnership with academia, local authorities, civil society organizations, international partners, and the private sector. Evidence-based policymaking guides our actions. Serbia has developed an integrated national road safety database, geolocated and publicly available. It's run by Road Traffic Safety Agency and it covers all local self-government units, enabling systematic monitoring of road safety performance, identification of risks, and evaluation of the effectiveness of implemented measures. Over the longer term, Serbia has recorded a positive trend in reducing road traffic fatalities. Annual fatalities have declined decline from around 900 before the adoption of the Law on Traffic Safety in 2009 to 599 in 2015 and 488 in 2025, despite the number of registered vehicles increasing from approximately 1.8 million to more than 3.1 million. Nevertheless, further efforts are needed to achieve our 2030 targets. Behind the data, behind every number, is a person, a family member, a trend, which is why we work towards Vision Zero. Every death on our roads is unacceptable. Therefore, Serbia remains committed to working together with all partners to accelerate progress towards safer mobility, because every life saved is a shared success. Thank you for your attention.

Thank you, Madam President. It is my singular honor to present the commitment of the Federal Republic of Nigeria under the leadership of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu GCFR in advancing global road safety. This whole government multi-sectoral strategy enjoys the full support of the federal government and is coordinated through the National Road Safety Advisory Council chaired by the Vice President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. Following Nigeria's accession to the 6th United Nations Convention, we have strengthened fleet safety and reinforce evidence-based road safety management through the National Crash Reporting Information System, NCRIS, while enhancing post-crash care with a state-of-the-art National Emergency Call Center and a 24-hour ambulance service to ensure prompt response to crashes. Nigeria also launched Nigeria Road Assessment Program, Nigeria RAP, in partnership with International Road Safety Assessment Program, IRAP, to advance the safe system approach and improve road infrastructure safety. While Nigeria has recorded significant progress, important gaps remain, particularly intelligent enforcement technologies, road infrastructure, safety assessment, and institutional capacity development. Nigeria therefore calls upon the international community to strengthen technical cooperation, facilitate technology transfer, and support sustainable capacity building initiatives to accelerate the achievement of our shared road safety goals and vision. Nigeria remains steadfast in making road safety a national priority. We reaffirm our support I thank you all for the outcomes of this meeting and pledge to continue working with partners to build safer roads, save more lives, and—
I thank the distinguished representative of Nigeria. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union, speaking on behalf of the EU and its member states.

President, Excellencies, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the European Union and its member states. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Albania, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Georgia, as well as Armenia, Andorra, San Marino, and the United Kingdom aligned themselves with this statement. We thank the President of the General Assembly for convening this important high-level meeting on improving global road safety. We also express our sincere appreciation to the co-facilitators, the Permanent Representatives of the Kyrgyz Republic and the Slovak Republic, for their dedicated efforts in guiding the negotiations towards a consensus-based progress declaration. The EU and its member states are pleased to support the adoption of the progress declaration today, and we remain firmly committed To the global target of halving road traffic deaths and serious injuries by 2030. Achieving this objective requires ambition, accountability, and effective implementation. Every day, more than 3,500 people lose their lives on the world's roads, while tens of millions more suffer injuries that often have lifelong consequences. Road traffic accidents remain one of the leading causes of death among children and young adults worldwide and disproportionately affect vulnerable road users, and low- and middle-income countries. These tragedies are preventable. They require sustained political commitment, effective policies, and collective action at all levels. The EU would like to highlight 3 priorities. First, while human error is inevitable, deaths and serious injuries are not. Road transport systems must be designed to anticipate human mistakes and ensure that they do not result in fatal or life-changing consequences. Experience has shown that lasting progress depends on comprehensive action. Safer infrastructure, high vehicle safety standards, appropriate speed management, effective enforcement of traffic rules, high-quality post-accident care, and evidence-based policymaking must all work together. Second, road safety is a shared responsibility. Governments, local authorities, civil society, the private sector, academia, and international organizations all have an essential role to play. No country can address this challenge alone. International cooperation, knowledge sharing, and strong multilateral partnerships remain indispensable for accelerating progress worldwide. The EU is committed to strengthening cooperation with the UN, the WHO, the UN Regional Commissions, and other international partners to promote the implementation of global road safety standards and support capacity building where it is needed most. Through the Global Gateway strategy, and other international partnerships, the EU supports sustainable transport infrastructure that integrates road safety from the earliest stages of planning and design. We also invest in technical assistance, institutional capacity building, and knowledge exchange to help partner countries develop effective and sustainable road safety systems. Finally, innovation and digital transformation offer significant opportunities to improve road safety. Connected mobility, intelligent transport systems, artificial intelligence, and better use of data can contribute to safer roads, more effective traffic management, and improved emergency response. At the same time, technology must complement, not replace, strong institutions, sound legislation, and responsible road user behavior. Particular attention must continue to be given to vulnerable road users, including pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities. Safe mobility should be accessible to everyone, and transport systems must be designed with the needs of all users in mind. President, colleagues, this high-level meeting should reinforce our collective determination to implement the commitments we have made. The lives behind these statistics remind us that road safety is ultimately about protecting people, strengthening communities, and promoting sustainable development. The EU stands ready to work with all partners to accelerate implementation, share experience, and mobilize the political will necessary to achieve our common objective: roads that are safe for everyone, everywhere. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the European Union. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Canada, speaking also on behalf of CANZUS.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to deliver the statement on behalf of Australia, New Zealand, and my own country, Canada. We thank the United Nations, the President of the General Assembly, the World Health Organization, the Secretary-General's Special Envoy for Road Safety, and all partners for convening this important high-level meeting on improving global road safety. Road safety is a public health, economic, and sustainable development priority. Every death and serious injury on our roads is preventable and carries profound consequences for individuals, families, communities, and societies. As we enter the second half of the Decade of Action for Road Safety, we must accelerate progress if we are to achieve the global target of reducing road traffic deaths and serious injuries by 50% by 2030. Canada, Australia, and New Zealand will do our part to help achieve that goal. We welcome the Declaration's focus on leadership, accountability, data, financing, implementation, and international cooperation. Meaningful progress will depend on sustained action grounded in evidence. While progress has been made, road traffic deaths and serious injuries continue to have devastating impacts on individuals, families, and communities. These challenges reinforce the need for renewed action, sustained investment, and strong partnerships. Our 3 countries continue to advance national road safety strategies grounded in the safe system approach and the long-term vision that no death, or serious injury on our roads is acceptable. Canada's Road Safety Strategy 2035+, Australia's New Road Safety Strategy 2021 to 2030, and New Zealand's Road Safety Objectives all recognize that while human error is inevitable, deaths and serious injuries are not. Across our countries, governments are working with regional and local authorities authorities, Indigenous communities, law enforcement, public health organizations, researchers, industry, and civil society partners to deliver better road safety outcomes. We recognize that road safety is a shared responsibility requiring action across all levels of government and society. We continue to support evidence-based measures to address key risk factors including impaired driving, fatigue, speeding, and distracted driving, while responding to emerging challenges across transportation systems. Data, research, and innovation remain central to our efforts. We are strengthening road safety data systems to better identify risks, measure performance, and support evidence-based decision-making. We appreciate the adoption of the Progress Declaration, which will help drive progress towards our collective road safety goals. That said, we are discouraged that it was not possible to adopt this resolution by consensus. Canada, Australia, and New Zealand have worked closely together throughout the negotiations of this declaration and on broader multilateral road safety efforts. We believe that international cooperation, shared expertise, and mutual learning are essential to accelerating progress and supporting implementation across all regions. As we enter the second half of the Decade of Action for Road Safety, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand will play our part and work with partners to strengthen implementation and save lives. Together, we can accelerate progress and build safer roads for everyone. Thank you.

Merci.
I thank the distinguished representative of Canada. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt.

Ladies and gentlemen, Egypt has adopted a comprehensive approach to enhance road safety that is based on improving infrastructure, enhancing institutional coordination, the National Project for Roads, and developing the bridges and improving infrastructure of existing roads, enhance connectivity across the country, and to prevent bottlenecks and traffic jams across the country. We continue to use intelligent systems and use technology in management of traffic and for enforcement, supporting also emergency and post-accident services. We reiterate that safety on roads requires a comprehensive approach that includes the safe design of roads, the safety of vehicles, as well as control on speed, as well as care after accidents. We need to give priority to 4 pathways in this sense. First, provide sustainable and affordable financing to countries to develop infrastructure and implement their national road safety strategies. Second, enhance technology transfer and build capacities of developing countries, particularly in smart transport as well as data systems and weak response frameworks. Support the development of data systems at the national level to understand the reasons for accidents and channel resources to address them. The smart traffic control and video monitoring system, which proved its efficiency in major cities, has been now scaled nationwide. To align our efforts with global standards, Kazakhstan launched a national road assessment program in close partnership with international road assessment program, the Kazakh Road Safety Research Institute is evaluating our infrastructure using the STAR rating system to bring our roads to a safer level. Additionally, Kazakhstan has joined the UN Global Information Campaign, Make a Safety Statement. It fosters further a national culture of safe behavior on the roads. Kazakhstan reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the UN targets. Our new national strategy, combined with cutting-edge technologies and robust interagency cooperation, will form the foundation of a resilient, sustainable system dedicated to achieving our shared goal: reducing by half road deaths and injuries by 2030. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kazakhstan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Paraguay.

Excellencies, the Philippines welcomes the adoption of the Progress Declaration on Improving Global Road Safety and reaffirms its steadfast commitment in making our roads safer for all. Road traffic injuries remain one of the world's leading public health and development challenges, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Beyond the tragic loss of lives, road crashes place immense strain on health systems, impede economic growth, and disproportionately affect the most vulnerable and at risk, including children, older persons, persons with disabilities, cyclists, motorcyclists, and low-income communities. In November 2022, the Philippines acceded to the UN 1958 Agreement on vehicle regulations to further align national vehicle safety standards with international UN regulations. We value our close cooperation with the WHO, UNICEF, and the UN Secretary-General's Special Envoy for Road Safety in advancing evidence-based, people-centered solutions. At the global level, the Philippines supports stronger international cooperation, particularly in capacity building, technology transfer, data systems and sustainable financing for low- and middle-income countries to accelerate progress towards safer mobility. Excellencies, the true measure of our commitment will not only be the declaration we just adopted, but the lives we save and protect. Let us match our shared ambition with sustained action so that safe mobility becomes a reality for all. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Philippines. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation.

Madam President, Russia has been consistent in its advocacy for enhancing international efforts to ensure road safety. We're proud of the fact that this issue has been among the chief priorities of the UN agenda. After all, it was our country in particular in 2011 that initiated the holding of the first ministerial conference on road safety in Moscow that laid the ground for forming a machinery of international cooperation in this area. We welcome the fact that this work is ongoing ongoing today as well, already in the context of the second decade for action on road safety in the period up to 2030. We trust that today's meeting will be an additional contribution toward further advancing this agenda. Russia has significant expert capacity in terms of enhancing road safety, and we are prepared to share it with all interested partners. Our country is a donor to the United Nations Road Safety Fund. With Russian financing support, a number of projects have already been implemented to curb mortality on the roads in the states of Central Asia. Speaking of national efforts, we want to note that the strengthening of road safety has been among the key priorities of state policy in Russia and is among the national development goals of our country. November of last year saw our President Putin adopt a corresponding strategy. It covered the period through 2030 and for the period beyond that to 2036. The document sets out a goal of decreasing by a factor of 1.5 the deaths in crashes by 2030, and we want to halve those deaths compared to 2023 levels by 2036. What's more, in May of this year, the Russian government adopted a plan for implementation of this strategy, which consists of a set of 266 measures. These seek to improve state administration in terms of road safety. The adoption of this strategy made— took road safety to a qualitatively new level, laying the ground for consolidation of political, financial, and staffing resources for achieving the aforementioned goals. Its implementation will allow us to build on existing gains and ensure a further reduction of road crashes. Most importantly, it will protect human lives and the health of our citizens. Today we can note that the Russian Federation is moving confidently toward the aforementioned milestones drawing on systemic changes and a comprehensive interagency approach. I thank you.
Distinguished representative of the Russian Federation, I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. Road safety is fundamentally a development and public health issue. Every serious road crash places immense pressure on emergency medical services, trauma care, rehabilitation systems, and national health budgets. Beyond the tragic loss of life, road traffic injuries diminish economic productivity, disrupt families, and undermine sustainable development. Reducing road traffic deaths and injuries is therefore integral to strengthening resilient health systems and advancing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, as well as Zimbabwe's Vision 2030. Despite progress in global road safety, fatalities remain unacceptably high. In Zimbabwe, a traffic crash occurs approximately every 15 minutes, More than 35,000 crashes are recorded annually, resulting in over 1,800 deaths and more than 10,000 injuries. Behind these statistics are lives lost, livelihoods disrupted, and national potential diminished. For many developing countries, these challenges are compounded by inadequate infrastructure, limited fiscal space, and the growing impact of climate change on climate— on transport networks. Road safety must therefore be pursued alongside investments in sustainable and climate-resilient infrastructure. In response, Zimbabwe is implementing comprehensive institutional and legislative reforms guided by its National Development Strategy and the recommendations of the Road Safety Performance Review. We are strengthening enforcement, modernizing transport systems, and enhancing public awareness and education. An integrated road traffic authority will soon be established to strengthen regulation and oversight. Zimbabwe is also developing smart technologies to improve road safety compliance, aligning its regulatory framework with international standards and operationalizing a road traffic fund— road accident fund to support post-crash medical care and survivors. Zimbabwe believes that road safety must be recognized as an integral component sustainable infrastructure financing. Investment in transport systems should be measured not only by the roads we build but by the lives we save. We therefore call for predictable financing, capacity building, and technology transfer to support nationally determined road safety priorities, particularly in developing countries. Zimbabwe remains committed to achieving SDG Target 3.6 and implementing the United Nations Decade of action for road safety. Together, let us build transport systems that are safe, resilient, and inclusive for all.

I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mauritius.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. The Republic of Mauritius fully aligns itself with the global target to halve road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030. Road safety remains a national priority for the Government of Mauritius. Mauritius recognizes that every life lost or injury sustained inflict severe, long-lasting social and economic consequences. Over the past 18 months, Mauritius has strengthened its legislative and enforcement frameworks on multiple fronts. Following the constructive visit of Mr. Jean Todt, the UN Secretary-General's Special Envoy for Road Safety, in April 2025, we officially launched the UN Global Campaign for road safety in Mauritius. Guided by his advice, we are currently reviewing our legislation regarding motorcycle helmet standards to better protect two-wheeler riders who are among the most vulnerable road users. We have successfully reintroduced the penalty point system to deter reckless driving. This system will adapt dynamically, utilizing data-driven adjustments to maximize road safety. Regulations have also been promulgated to strictly monitor oversized structures used in public processions. In our continuous effort to modernize enforcement, we are transitioning from standard automated speed cameras to advanced integrated safe city cameras. At the same time, legislative amendments are underway to allow for the impoundment of vehicles when drivers are found operating under influence of drugs or alcohol. And a legal framework will soon be established in regard to electric cycles and scooters. Guided by the Safe System Approach, Mauritius is also finalizing its National Road Safety Strategy 2026-2030. The strategy will provide for an evidence-based framework aimed at reducing road traffic fatalities through strengthened institutional coordination, safer infrastructure, safer vehicles, and enhanced post-crash response. It will also embed robust road safety education into our primary and secondary school curricula. Madam President, achieving the ambitious target of the second decade of action requires sustainable financing technological innovation, and robust capacity building. For SIDS in particular, continued international cooperation, technical assistance, knowledge sharing, and targeted financial support remain indispensable.
